sources.title: A Modest Proposal (selections)
sources.author: Jonathan Swift
sources.citation: Jonathan Swift, A Modest Proposal for preventing the children of poor people in Ireland, from being a burden on their parents or country, and for making them beneficial to the publick (Dublin, 1729). Text from Project Gutenberg eBook 1080.
sources.context: Written in 1729 while Swift was Dean of St Patrick's in Dublin, the pamphlet adopts the voice of a reasonable 'projector' and proposes that the poor sell their infants as food. It was published anonymously, and some readers took it for a serious scheme.
questions: What does the projector claim as his only motive, and what does the reader understand it to be?
Which real remedies does the speaker reject, and what does that rejection reveal about the pamphlet's target?
The proposal is written in the calm language of arithmetic and public benefit. Why is that tone more disturbing than open anger would be?

sources.title: The Rape of the Lock (selections)
sources.author: Alexander Pope
sources.citation: Alexander Pope, The Rape of the Lock: An Heroi-Comical Poem, in The Rape of the Lock, and Other Poems (1714). Text from Project Gutenberg eBook 9800.
sources.context: Pope wrote the poem after Lord Petre cut a lock of Arabella Fermor's hair and the two families quarrelled. The 1714 version adds the 'machinery' of the sylphs. The selections come from Cantos I, II, III, and V.
questions: What does Pope gain by describing a card game and a haircut in the language of epic war?
The sylphs are called the 'machinery.' What does their presence add to the poem's irony?
Clarissa's speech in Canto V offers the poem's one piece of plain good sense. Why does Pope have no one applaud her?

sources.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (selections)
sources.author: Mark Twain
sources.citation: Mark Twain, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (New York: Charles L. Webster and Company, 1885; first published 1884). Text from Project Gutenberg eBook 76.
sources.context: Huck narrates his own story in dialect and never signals a joke. In the selections he submits to being 'sivilized,' and later, believing he will be damned for helping Jim escape, he tears up the letter that would return Jim to slavery.
questions: Huck believes he is choosing damnation. What does the reader understand that he does not?
How does Huck's ungrammatical, matter-of-fact voice make the moral crisis sharper rather than softer?
A narrator is unreliable when the account disagrees with the norms the book establishes. In what sense is Huck unreliable here — about facts, or about himself?

interpretations.claim: Booth argued that a stable irony invites the reader to reconstruct an intended meaning beneath the literal surface, and that the reconstruction succeeds only within a community that shares the assumptions the irony relies on. The reader is not free to invent any meaning; the author's signals, and the shared norms of the audience, guide the correction.
interpretations.note: Later theorists questioned whether an intended meaning can always be recovered, and whether some ironies are deliberately undecidable rather than stable. Booth's account is a description of how most irony works, not a proof that every ironic text has one recoverable sense.

interpretations.claim: Muecke described irony as a 'two-storey' phenomenon: an innocent or literal surface concealing a real meaning beneath, with the reader moving between the two levels. He classified its forms — verbal, dramatic, situational, and cosmic — and the attitudes, from playful to bitter, that a writer may take toward the gap.
interpretations.note: Muecke's taxonomy is descriptive; it maps the varieties of irony without explaining how a reader detects them. Booth's work, by contrast, concentrates on the interpretive process and on the signals that let a reader decide that irony is present at all.

activities.prompt: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker…
choices: says one thing and means the opposite, expecting to be understood
lies in order to deceive the listener
reports events out of their chronological order
uses a metaphor to describe an abstraction
activities.feedback: The ironist does not intend to deceive; the ironist intends to be understood, and assumes the audience is in on the joke.

activities.prompt: In dramatic irony, who knows more than the character does?
choices: the audience or reader
the character himself
no one at all
only the author, and never the reader
activities.feedback: In Oedipus Tyrannus the audience knows who the murderer is, and hears the second meaning in Oedipus's vow that he cannot hear.

activities.prompt: Socratic irony is best described as…
choices: feigned ignorance used as a method of questioning
a savage attack on private vice
a coincidence that reverses expectation
praise that is really blame
activities.feedback: Socrates claims to know nothing and by questions exposes the contradictions in those who are certain; the ignorance is a method, not a lie.

activities.prompt: Which pairing matches the two classical modes of satire?
choices: Horatian is gentle and corrective; Juvenalian is savage and punishing
Horatian is savage and punishing; Juvenalian is gentle and corrective
Both are gentle; the difference is only of metre
Both are savage; the difference is only of length
activities.feedback: Horace laughs at folly, himself included; Juvenal rages at a corrupt world and aims to expose rather than to correct.

activities.prompt: Whom does A Modest Proposal finally attack?
choices: the comfortable landlords and politicians who treat the poor as a burden
the poor themselves
the French
the Catholic clergy alone
activities.feedback: The projector dismisses every real remedy as visionary because it would cost the comfortable something, and the pamphlet's anger falls on them.

activities.prompt: What is the 'machinery' in The Rape of the Lock?
choices: the supernatural sylphs and gnomes who attend the heroine
the coach and horses that carry Belinda
the printing press that produced the poem
the epic similes in the final canto
activities.feedback: Pope borrowed the term from the critics for the part played by deities in an epic, and built his out of the Rosicrucian spirits of the air.

activities.prompt: Why is the opening sentence of Pride and Prejudice ironic?
choices: It states as a universal truth a wish held by the neighbourhood's mothers
It is spoken aloud by Mrs. Bennet
It contains a factual error about the law
It praises a man the novel later shows to be poor
activities.feedback: The sentence has the form of a general truth and the content of a local wish: it is the mothers who want a rich husband, not the man who wants a wife.

activities.prompt: In the passage from Huckleberry Finn, Huck is an unreliable narrator because…
choices: his judgment of his own act is the opposite of the book's moral judgment
he cannot remember the events he describes
he tells the story out of chronological order
he is a child and invents the whole episode
activities.feedback: Huck believes he is damning himself; the reader knows he is choosing decency. He is unreliable about himself, not about the facts.

activities.prompt: Why is Daniel Defoe's The Shortest Way with the Dissenters (1702) important for the study of irony?
choices: Its irony was not caught, and Defoe was punished for a position he opposed
It was the first English poem written in heroic couplets
It was the model for Pope's mock-epic
It proved that irony never depends on the reader
activities.feedback: The pamphlet was read literally by readers on both sides, and Defoe was arrested, pilloried, and imprisoned — evidence that irony is a contract that can fail.

activities.prompt: Using the passage, explain how a reader can know that Swift does not mean what the projector says, and what the pamphlet is really attacking.
activities.context: "I have been assured by a very knowing American of my acquaintance in London, that a young healthy child well nursed, is, at a year old, a most delicious nourishing and wholesome food... I profess in the sincerity of my heart, that I have not the least personal interest in endeavouring to promote this necessary work, having no other motive than the publick good of my country... I have no children, by which I can propose to get a single penny; the youngest being nine years old, and my wife past child-bearing." — Jonathan Swift, A Modest Proposal (1729)
rubric: identifies a signal of irony, such as the calm tone, the arithmetic, or the profession of disinterest
explains what the pamphlet really attacks, such as the landlords or the treatment of the poor
uses a specific phrase from the passage as evidence
